mainEntity.name: What are Wrapper Classes in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wrapper classes in Java are object representations of the 8 primitive data types. Each primitive has a corresponding wrapper class in java.lang: byte → Byte, short → Short, int → Integer, long → Long, float → Float, double → Double, char → Character, boolean → Boolean. Wrapper classes are needed when you must use an object where a primitive is not allowed — such as in Java Collections (List<Integer> instead of List<int>), with Generics, with null values, or when using utility methods like Integer.parseInt(). They are immutable and final classes.

mainEntity.name: What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Autoboxing is the automatic conversion by the Java compiler of a primitive value to its corresponding wrapper class object — e.g., int → Integer, double → Double. Unboxing is the reverse — automatic conversion of a wrapper object back to its primitive — e.g., Integer → int. Example: Integer a = 5; is autoboxing (compiler calls Integer.valueOf(5)); int b = a; is unboxing (compiler calls a.intValue()). Introduced in Java 5. Autoboxing enables using primitives seamlessly in Collections and Generics without explicit wrapping. Key risk: unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException.

mainEntity.name: What is Integer caching in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java caches Integer objects in the range -128 to 127 (inclusive). When you autobox or call Integer.valueOf() for values in this range, Java returns the same cached object — so == comparison returns true. For values outside this range, new Integer objects are created — == returns false even for equal values. Example: Integer a = 127; Integer b = 127; System.out.println(a == b); // true (cached). Integer x = 128; Integer y = 128; System.out.println(x == y); // false (not cached). This is why you must always use .equals() to compare Integer values, never ==. The same caching applies to Byte, Short, Long (-128 to 127) and Boolean (TRUE/FALSE cached).

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between int and Integer in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: int is a primitive data type — stored directly on the stack, cannot be null, no methods, default value 0, fastest and most memory-efficient. Integer is a wrapper class object — stored on the heap, can be null, has utility methods (parseInt, valueOf, compareTo, etc.), default value null for fields, used in Collections and Generics. int cannot be used as a generic type parameter (List<int> is invalid) — use List<Integer>. Integer can be null — assigning null and unboxing throws NullPointerException. Use int when performance matters; use Integer when you need an object, nullable value, or utility methods.

mainEntity.name: How do you convert String to int in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use Integer.parseInt(String) to convert a String to a primitive int: int n = Integer.parseInt('42'); — throws NumberFormatException if the string is not a valid integer. Use Integer.valueOf(String) to get an Integer object: Integer n = Integer.valueOf('42');. For the reverse — int to String — use: String s = String.valueOf(42); or String s = Integer.toString(42); or String s = 42 + ''; (concatenation, less preferred). Always wrap parseInt in try-catch when the input may not be a valid number.

articleHeader.title: Java Wrapper Classes — Autoboxing, Unboxing, Methods & Best Practices
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Java Wrapper Classes — what they are, why they exist, autoboxing and unboxing, Integer cache trap, parsing and conversion methods, usage in Collections and Generics, performance pitfalls, and real-world production code examples.

sections.title: What are Wrapper Classes in Java?

blocks.text: In Java, primitive types — int, double, boolean, char, byte, short, long, float — are not objects. They are raw values stored directly in memory for maximum performance. However, Java's object-oriented ecosystem — including Collections, Generics, and many APIs — requires objects, not primitives. Wrapper classes solve this: each primitive type has a corresponding class in java.lang that wraps the primitive value in an object.

Wrapper classes serve three main purposes: (1) Allow primitives to be used as objects — e.g., storing int values in a List<Integer>. (2) Provide utility methods for parsing, converting, and comparing values — e.g., Integer.parseInt(), Double.isNaN(). (3) Allow primitives to represent the null state — useful when absence of a value must be distinguished from zero or false. All wrapper classes are in the java.lang package (auto-imported), are immutable, and are declared final (cannot be subclassed).

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Wrapper Classes — 8 Primitives & Their Wrappers
blocks.text: byte → Byte | short → Short | int → Integer | long → Long | float → Float | double → Double | char → Character | boolean → Boolean. All wrapper classes are in java.lang (no import needed). All are immutable — once created, the value cannot change. All extend java.lang.Number (except Boolean and Character). All implement Comparable<T>. Key utility methods available: parseXxx(), valueOf(), xxxValue(), compareTo(), toString(), MAX_VALUE, MIN_VALUE constants.
Understanding when to use a primitive and when to use its wrapper class is fundamental to writing correct, performant Java. The table below summarizes all key differences.

Autoboxing is the automatic conversion of a primitive to its corresponding wrapper class, performed by the Java compiler. Unboxing is the reverse — automatic conversion from a wrapper object back to a primitive. Introduced in Java 5, these conversions happen transparently wherever a primitive is used where an object is expected, or vice versa. Under the hood, the compiler inserts calls to Integer.valueOf() for boxing and intValue() for unboxing.

blocks.label: AutoboxingUnboxing.java
lines: // Compiler translates to: Integer wrappedInt = Integer.valueOf(42);
// Compiler translates to: int unboxed = boxed.intValue();
int first = numbers.get(0);  // Unboxing: Integer → int
int sum = a + b;  // Both unboxed to int, then added
printValue(99);  // int autoboxed to Integer for method param
// int x = nullInt;  // NPE! nullInt.intValue() on null

blocks.title: ⚠️ Autoboxing Pitfall — Unboxing null Causes NPE
blocks.text: The most dangerous autoboxing pitfall: unboxing a null wrapper type throws NullPointerException. Example: Integer count = null; int x = count; — NPE! Common scenario: Map<String, Integer> map; int val = map.get('missing'); — map.get() returns null for missing key, unboxing null → NPE. Fix: always check wrapper types for null before unboxing, or use getOrDefault() for maps. The compiler inserts the intValue() call silently — the NPE appears as if from the assignment line, which is confusing for beginners.

Integer is the most commonly used wrapper class. It wraps the primitive int and provides a rich set of static and instance methods for parsing, converting, comparing, and performing bitwise operations on integer values.

items.title: Creating Integer Objects
items.text: Integer.valueOf(int) — preferred factory method; uses cache for -128 to 127. Integer.valueOf(String) — parses string to Integer object. new Integer(int) — deprecated since Java 9; use valueOf() instead. Autoboxing: Integer i = 42; — compiler calls Integer.valueOf(42) automatically.

items.title: Parsing & Converting
items.text: Integer.parseInt(String) — parses String to primitive int. Throws NumberFormatException if invalid. Integer.parseInt(String, radix) — parse in given base (2 for binary, 16 for hex). Integer.toString(int) — int to String. Integer.toBinaryString(int) — decimal to binary string. Integer.toHexString(int) — decimal to hex string. Integer.toOctalString(int) — decimal to octal string.

items.title: Comparison & Math Utilities
items.text: Integer.compare(x, y) — compare two ints; returns negative/0/positive. Integer.max(a, b) — larger of two ints. Integer.min(a, b) — smaller of two ints. Integer.sum(a, b) — sum (useful as method reference). Integer.MAX_VALUE — 2147483647. Integer.MIN_VALUE — -2147483648. intValue() — extract primitive int from Integer object. compareTo(Integer) — instance comparison.

blocks.label: IntegerClass.java
lines: Integer a = Integer.valueOf(100);     // Preferred — uses cache
Integer b = Integer.valueOf("200");   // Parse string → Integer
int hex = Integer.parseInt("1F", 16); // Parse hex string
int bin = Integer.parseInt("1010", 2); // Parse binary string
long asLong   = wrapped.longValue();  // Widening via wrapper

blocks.text: Double and Float are wrapper classes for double and float primitives respectively. They include essential utility methods for parsing decimal strings, checking for special floating-point values like NaN (Not a Number) and Infinity, and performing comparisons. Double is the more commonly used of the two, as double is preferred over float in modern Java for its precision.

blocks.label: DoubleFloatClass.java
lines: Double d2 = Double.valueOf("2.718");  // Parse string → Double
// ❌ NaN != NaN in Java — use isNaN() to check

blocks.title: ⚠️ NaN Is Never Equal to Itself
blocks.text: Double.NaN == Double.NaN returns false — this is by IEEE 754 floating-point standard, which Java follows. This is the only value in Java that is not equal to itself. Always use Double.isNaN(value) to check for NaN, never == Double.NaN. Similarly, Float.isNaN(value) for float. This trips up many developers who expect == to work for NaN as it does for all other values.

Boolean is the wrapper class for the boolean primitive. It is the simplest wrapper class — holding only two meaningful states: Boolean.TRUE and Boolean.FALSE. Like all wrapper classes, it allows boolean values to be used in Collections, Generics, and nullable contexts. Boolean also provides useful methods for parsing boolean strings and logical operations.

blocks.label: BooleanClass.java
lines: System.out.println(b1 + " " + b2 + " " + b3 + " " + b4); // true true false false
Boolean obj = Boolean.valueOf("true");   // Returns Boolean object
Boolean enabled = null; // null = unknown/not set
// if (nullBool) { }  // NPE! unboxing null Boolean → boolean

blocks.title: 💡 Boolean.TRUE.equals() — Null-Safe Boolean Check
blocks.text: When working with nullable Boolean objects, never unbox them directly in an if-condition: if (booleanObj) throws NPE if null. Use Boolean.TRUE.equals(booleanObj) — this is null-safe because TRUE.equals(null) returns false, not NPE. Similarly Boolean.FALSE.equals(booleanObj) for false check. Also note: Boolean.parseBoolean(null) returns false without throwing NPE — making it safe for parsing potentially absent config values.

Character is the wrapper class for the char primitive. It provides a comprehensive set of static utility methods for testing and transforming individual characters — checking if a character is a letter, digit, whitespace, uppercase, lowercase, and converting between cases. These methods are Unicode-aware, handling characters from all scripts correctly.

blocks.label: CharacterClass.java
lines: int ascii = (int) ch1;        // Cast to int: 65

blocks.text: Long, Short, and Byte follow the same pattern as Integer — each wraps its corresponding primitive, provides parsing and conversion methods, and exposes numeric constants. Long is commonly used for timestamps, IDs, and file sizes where int's range is insufficient. Short and Byte are rarely used in modern application code but appear in low-level I/O and data protocol handling.

blocks.label: LongShortByteClass.java
lines: Long timestamp = now;  // Autoboxing to Long
// ── Long caching — same as Integer: -128 to 127 ─────────────────
// ── Number superclass methods — available on all numeric wrappers

blocks.text: One of the most famous and confusing Java interview topics: the Integer cache. The JVM caches Integer objects for values in the range -128 to 127. When autoboxing or calling Integer.valueOf() for values in this range, Java returns the same cached object. For values outside this range, a new object is created each time. This means == comparison on Integer objects gives true for small values and false for large ones — a behavior that looks random and baffles many developers.

blocks.label: IntegerCache.java
lines: Integer b = 100;  // Same cached object returned
System.out.println(x == y);       // true  (127 is in cache)
Integer p = 128;  // Autoboxing → Integer.valueOf(128) → NEW object
// ❌ NEVER use == to compare Integer (or any wrapper) values
// ── Same caching applies to Long, Short, Byte ────────────────────

blocks.title: ⚠️ Integer Cache — The Golden Rule
blocks.text: NEVER use == to compare Integer, Long, Short, or Byte objects for value equality. Always use .equals(). The cache makes == appear to work for small values (-128 to 127) but silently fail for larger ones — one of the most deceptive bugs in Java. Caching summary: Integer, Short, Byte, Long → cache -128 to 127. Character → caches 0 to 127. Boolean → always caches (only TRUE and FALSE exist). Double and Float → NO caching (infinite possible values). The JVM may extend Integer cache upper bound via -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=N JVM flag.

blocks.text: Parsing and conversion between String, primitive types, and wrapper objects is one of the most frequent operations in Java programs — reading user input, parsing configuration values, converting API responses, and building display strings. Each wrapper class provides a consistent set of methods for these conversions.

blocks.text: The most fundamental reason wrapper classes exist in everyday Java code is their role in Collections and Generics. Java generics work only with reference types — you cannot write List<int> or Map<String, double>. Wrapper classes bridge this gap, letting you store primitives in type-safe collections. With autoboxing, the conversion is mostly invisible — but understanding what happens under the hood prevents performance mistakes and NPE surprises.

sections.title: Autoboxing Performance — When to Avoid It

blocks.text: Autoboxing is convenient but not free. Each boxing operation allocates a new object on the heap (outside the -128 to 127 cache range), and each unboxing call adds a method invocation. In tight loops or high-throughput code, excessive autoboxing creates unnecessary garbage that increases GC pressure and degrades performance. Understanding where autoboxing happens implicitly is key to writing efficient Java.

blocks.label: AutoboxingPerformance.java
lines: // ❌ BAD: Autoboxing in tight loop — creates millions of Integer objects
Long sum = 0L;  // Long wrapper — not primitive long!
sum += i;  // Unbox sum, add i (autobox i too), rebox result
// Creates a new Long object on every iteration!
// ✅ GOOD: Use primitive — zero boxing overhead
sum += i;  // Pure primitive arithmetic — no objects
// ❌ BAD: List<Integer> for large numeric datasets
// ✅ BETTER: int[] for pure numeric data
arr[i] = i; // No objects — just array of primitives
// ✅ BETTER: IntStream for stream operations on int data
// ✅ RULE: Use primitives for local variables, fields, and method parameters
//         in performance-sensitive code. Use wrappers only when needed:
//         Collections, Generics, null-check scenarios, utility methods.

blocks.title: 💡 Autoboxing Performance Rule of Thumb
blocks.text: Use primitives (int, long, double) by default for: local variables, method parameters, return types, and class fields where null is not needed. Use wrapper classes (Integer, Long, Double) only when: storing in Collections/Maps, using with Generics, null is a valid state, calling utility methods. For stream operations on large int/long/double datasets, prefer IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream — they avoid boxing entirely. The single most common autoboxing performance bug: declaring a sum variable as Long instead of long in a loop.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns represent common misuses of wrapper classes in professional Java code. Each one introduces bugs, performance degradation, or design problems that are hard to debug.

items.title: Using new Integer() / new Double() — Deprecated Constructors
items.text: new Integer(42), new Double(3.14), new Boolean(true) — all constructors on wrapper classes are deprecated since Java 9 and may be removed in a future release. They always create new heap objects, bypassing the Integer cache. Use Integer.valueOf(42), Double.valueOf(3.14), Boolean.valueOf(true), or simply autoboxing (Integer i = 42). Deprecated constructors are an easy item to flag in code reviews and interviews.

items.title: Using == to Compare Wrapper Objects
items.text: Integer a = 1000; Integer b = 1000; if (a == b) is reference comparison — not value comparison. It returns true accidentally for -128 to 127 (cached) and false for larger values, creating subtle bugs that only appear with certain data. Rule: always use .equals() or Integer.compare(a, b) for Integer value comparison. This is one of the most tested Java gotchas in interviews at all levels.

items.title: Using Wrapper Types in Performance-Critical Loops
items.text: Declaring Long sum = 0L in a loop that iterates millions of times creates a new Long object on every iteration (outside the cache range). This floods the heap and triggers GC. In any loop or computation-heavy method, use primitive types by default. Upgrade to wrapper only when you need the value in a Collection, need null, or need utility methods. Profile first — but the rule 'primitives in loops' is almost always correct.

items.title: Calling get() on Map Without Null Check Then Unboxing
items.text: map.get(key) returns null for missing keys. Immediately unboxing the result to a primitive — int val = map.get(key) — causes NPE when the key is missing. Always use getOrDefault(key, defaultValue) for maps with primitive value types, or store the result in an Integer first and check for null before unboxing. This is extremely common in code reviews and is a reliable source of production NPEs.

items.title: Ignoring NumberFormatException in parseInt()
items.text: Integer.parseInt() throws NumberFormatException for any non-numeric input including empty strings, strings with spaces, null strings, or strings with letters. In production code that parses user input or external data, always wrap parseInt() in try-catch or validate the string first. Never assume external input is a valid number. Consider utility methods like Apache Commons' NumberUtils.toIntOrDefault() for safer parsing in complex applications.

items.title: Using Wrapper Fields Instead of Primitives Without Reason
items.text: Declaring class fields as Integer age; instead of int age; when null is never a meaningful state adds unnecessary complexity — field can accidentally become null and cause NPE on access. Use primitive fields (int, double, boolean) as the default; switch to wrapper (Integer, Double, Boolean) only when null is a genuinely meaningful state that must be distinguished from zero or false. Document the null meaning with a comment when you do use wrapper fields.

sections.title: Java Wrapper Classes Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java developer interviews at all levels — from campus placements to senior engineer rounds. Wrapper classes, autoboxing, and Integer caching are high-frequency topics.

items.q: Q1. What are Wrapper Classes in Java? Why are they needed?
items.a: Wrapper classes are object representations of Java's 8 primitive types: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean. They are needed because: (1) Java Collections and Generics work only with objects — List<Integer> is valid, List<int> is not. (2) Utility methods for parsing, converting, and comparing — Integer.parseInt(), Double.isNaN(). (3) Null representation — Integer can be null; int cannot. (4) Reflection and APIs that expect Object type. All wrapper classes are in java.lang (auto-imported), are immutable, and final. They extend Number (except Boolean and Character) and implement Comparable<T>.

items.q: Q2. What is autoboxing and unboxing? Give examples.
items.a: Autoboxing is automatic primitive → wrapper conversion by the Java compiler. Unboxing is automatic wrapper → primitive conversion. Introduced in Java 5. Examples: Integer a = 5 is autoboxing (compiler inserts Integer.valueOf(5)). int b = a is unboxing (compiler inserts a.intValue()). Autoboxing in collections: list.add(42) — int 42 autoboxed to Integer.valueOf(42). Unboxing in arithmetic: Integer x = 10; Integer y = 20; int sum = x + y — both unboxed, added, result is primitive. Key risk: unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException. Performance risk: autoboxing in tight loops creates excessive heap objects.

items.q: Q3. What is Integer caching in Java? What is the output of Integer a = 128; Integer b = 128; System.out.println(a == b)?
items.a: Java caches Integer objects for values -128 to 127 via Integer.IntegerCache. Integer.valueOf() and autoboxing return the same cached object for values in this range. For 128 (outside cache), two separate objects are created — a == b compares references, so it prints false. a.equals(b) would print true. The cache range is a JVM optimization that cannot be changed at runtime except for the upper bound via -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=N. The same caching applies to Byte, Short, Long (-128 to 127) and Character (0-127). Boolean always returns TRUE or FALSE constants. Double and Float have no cache. Rule: always use .equals() to compare wrapper values, never ==.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between int and Integer in Java?
items.a: int: primitive, stored on stack, cannot be null, default value 0, no methods, ~4 bytes, fastest performance. Integer: object, stored on heap, can be null, default value null (for fields), has methods (parseInt, valueOf, compareTo), ~16 bytes + GC overhead. Cannot use int as generic type parameter (List<int> invalid) — must use Integer. int comparison with == works correctly; Integer comparison with == only works for cached range (-128 to 127). Use int for local variables, parameters, computations; use Integer for Collections, nullable values, and utility method access.

items.q: Q5. What does Integer.parseInt() do? How is it different from Integer.valueOf()?
items.a: Integer.parseInt(String s) parses the string and returns a primitive int. Throws NumberFormatException for invalid input. Returns int — no object. Integer.valueOf(String s) parses the string and returns an Integer object. Uses cache for -128 to 127. Returns Integer — an object. Integer.valueOf(int i) wraps a primitive int in an Integer object (uses cache). parseInt is preferred when you need a primitive result — slightly faster since no boxing. valueOf is needed when you require an Integer object. Both throw NumberFormatException on invalid strings. null input to parseInt throws NumberFormatException; Boolean.parseBoolean(null) is special — returns false without throwing.

items.q: Q6. Can you store null in a List<Integer>? What happens when you unbox it?
items.a: Yes — List<Integer> allows null elements (ArrayList does not prohibit null). Adding null: list.add(null) works fine. Retrieving and unboxing null: int val = list.get(index) where the element is null throws NullPointerException — unboxing null triggers intValue() on null. Similarly, iterating List<Integer> with for (int n : list) will NPE on any null element. Fix: filter nulls before processing — list.stream().filter(Objects::nonNull). Note: List.of() does NOT allow null — throws NullPointerException immediately on null element.

items.q: Q7. Why is new Integer(42) deprecated? What should you use instead?
items.a: new Integer(42) is deprecated since Java 9 for two reasons: (1) It always creates a new heap object — it bypasses the Integer cache, wasting memory even for small values. (2) The object is not shared with the cached pool, so Integer caching optimizations don't apply. Use Integer.valueOf(42) instead — it returns a cached object for -128 to 127, and a new object only for values outside the cache range. Or use autoboxing: Integer i = 42 — the compiler calls Integer.valueOf() automatically. The same deprecation applies to new Double(), new Boolean(), new Long(), etc.

Output: true, false, true. a == b: true — 127 is in the Integer cache (-128 to 127). Both a and b point to the same cached Integer object. == compares references — same object, so true. c == d: false — 128 is outside the cache range. Integer.valueOf(128) creates a new object each time. c and d are different objects. == compares references — different objects, so false. c.equals(d): true — equals() compares integer values, not references. Both hold value 128, so equals() returns true. Key lesson: never use == for Integer value comparison; always use .equals().

items.q: Q9. What happens when you do: Integer i = null; int j = i; Explain with Java 14+ message.
items.a: NullPointerException is thrown on line int j = i. Auto-unboxing calls i.intValue() internally. Since i is null, this is equivalent to null.intValue() — NPE. Java 14+ helpful message: 'Cannot unbox null value'. This is one of the most common NPE causes in code that mixes Integer and int. Typical production scenario: int score = map.get('key') where key is missing — map.get() returns null, unboxing null Integer to int throws NPE. Fix: Integer result = map.get('key'); int score = result != null ? result : 0; or map.getOrDefault('key', 0).

items.q: Q10. Are wrapper classes thread-safe? Can they be used in concurrent code?
items.a: Wrapper classes (Integer, Double, Boolean, etc.) are immutable — they cannot be modified after creation. Immutability makes them inherently thread-safe: multiple threads can read the same Integer object without synchronization because the value never changes. However, wrapper types themselves do not provide atomic operations. If you need to perform compound operations (read-modify-write) on a numeric value shared between threads — like a counter — use AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, or AtomicReference<Double> from java.util.concurrent.atomic. A local Integer variable or a field that is only ever assigned (not modified) is safe to use in concurrent code without additional synchronization.

sections.title: Practice Questions — Test Your Wrapper Class Knowledge

blocks.text: Challenge yourself with these practice questions. Attempt each independently before reading the answer — active recall is proven to be 2–3x more effective than passive reading.

items.a: Output: true, false, true. a == b: true — 100 is within Integer cache range (-128 to 127), both variables point to the same cached object. c == d: false — 200 is outside the cache range, two separate Integer objects are created by valueOf(), == compares different references. c.equals(d): true — equals() compares the integer value (200 == 200), not the object reference. Takeaway: never use == to compare Integer values; always use equals() or Integer.compare().

Compiles fine. At runtime: prints 1, then throws NullPointerException on the null element. The enhanced for-loop on List<Integer> unboxes each element to int via intValue(). For 1 → 1 (prints fine). For null → null.intValue() → NPE. Java 14+ message: 'Cannot unbox null value'. Fix: use Integer n instead of int n in the loop, or filter nulls first: list.stream().filter(Objects::nonNull).forEach(System.out::println).

Bug: Long sum = 0L declares a wrapper object. On every iteration of sum += i, the following happens: (1) sum is unboxed to primitive long, (2) i is added, (3) result is reboxed to a new Long object. For n = 10,000,000, this creates 10 million Long objects — massive GC pressure. Fix: change Long to long (primitive): public long sumRange(int n) { long sum = 0L; for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) { sum += i; } return sum; }. This is a famous Java performance anti-pattern, often called 'accidental autoboxing in a loop'. It can make code 10-20x slower.

Output: 2, 255, 1010, ff. parseInt('10', 2): interprets '10' as binary (base 2) = 1×2 + 0×1 = 2. parseInt('FF', 16): interprets 'FF' as hexadecimal = 15×16 + 15 = 255. toBinaryString(10): converts decimal 10 to binary string = '1010'. toHexString(255): converts decimal 255 to hex string = 'ff' (lowercase). These base-conversion methods are useful for low-level programming and bit manipulation tasks.

Issues: aliceScore = map.get('Alice') works (95 is non-null, unboxing safe). carolScore = map.get('Carol') — key absent, returns null, unboxing null → NPE. bobScore = map.get('Bob') — value IS null (not absent), unboxing null → NPE. Note: getOrDefault('Bob', 0) also returns null here because the value stored IS null (not a missing key). Fix: Integer aliceObj = studentScores.get('Alice'); int aliceScore = aliceObj != null ? aliceObj : 0; Integer carolObj = studentScores.get('Carol'); int carolScore = carolObj != null ? carolObj : 0; Integer bobObj = studentScores.get('Bob'); int bobScore = bobObj != null ? bobObj : 0; Or use getOrDefault only for missing-key scenarios, and explicit null checks for null-valued entries.

Output: true, true, true, false, false, false, false. Boolean.parseBoolean returns true ONLY when the string is 'true' in any case (equalsIgnoreCase('true')). Every other string — 'yes', '1', 'on', empty string, null — returns false without throwing an exception. This surprises many developers who expect 'yes', 'Y', or '1' to return true (as in many other languages or frameworks). Always explicitly document what string values your config/API accepts for boolean fields. If you need to accept 'yes'/'no', write a custom parser.

Bug: price > 0.0 unboxes price to double — if price is null, this throws NullPointerException. The comparison operator > triggers unboxing (price.doubleValue()), which NPEs on null. Fix A — null check first: if (price != null && price > 0.0) { applyDiscount(price); }. Fix B — use Optional: Optional.ofNullable(price).filter(p -> p > 0.0).ifPresent(this::applyDiscount);. Fix C — return primitive double from getProductPrice() if null is not meaningful (return 0.0 for unknown). Always be aware that comparison operators (<, >, <=, >=) on wrapper types trigger unboxing — null wrappers will NPE silently in comparisons.

Line A: false — 1000 is outside Integer cache range, two separate objects, == is reference comparison. Line B: true — equals() compares values, 1000 == 1000. Line C: true — a and b are unboxed primitives (int), == on primitives compares values directly. 1000 == 1000 is true. Line D: true — y + 0 is an arithmetic expression with a primitive int (0). This triggers unboxing of y to primitive int, the result (1000) is a primitive int. Comparing Integer x with a primitive int triggers unboxing of x too. So it becomes 1000 == 1000 (primitive comparison) — true. Key insight: any arithmetic operation on a wrapper produces a primitive result, making subsequent == a primitive (value) comparison.

sections.title: Conclusion — Wrapper Classes: Bridge Between Primitives and Objects

blocks.text: Wrapper classes are the bridge between Java's two type systems — the primitive world of int, double, and boolean, and the object world of Collections, Generics, and APIs. Autoboxing makes this bridge nearly invisible in day-to-day code, but professional Java developers understand exactly what happens under the hood — because the invisible conversions are precisely where the most subtle bugs and performance problems hide.

The two most important rules to internalize: (1) Always use .equals() — never == — to compare wrapper values, because Integer caching makes == deceptively correct for small values and silently wrong for large ones. (2) Prefer primitives by default — use wrapper classes only when Collections, Generics, null, or utility methods require them. Getting these two rules right eliminates the majority of wrapper-related bugs and performance problems in Java codebases.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Wrapper Classes

items.q: What are Wrapper Classes in Java?
items.a: Wrapper classes in Java are object representations of the 8 primitive data types: byte → Byte, short → Short, int → Integer, long → Long, float → Float, double → Double, char → Character, boolean → Boolean. They are needed for Collections and Generics (which require objects), for utility methods like Integer.parseInt(), and when null must represent absence of a value. All wrapper classes are in java.lang, are immutable, and are declared final.

items.q: What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?
items.a: Autoboxing is the automatic conversion of a primitive to its wrapper class object by the Java compiler — e.g., int → Integer. Unboxing is the reverse — wrapper → primitive. The compiler inserts Integer.valueOf() for boxing and intValue() for unboxing. Key risk: unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException. Introduced in Java 5. Performance risk: autoboxing in tight loops creates excess objects.

items.q: What is Integer caching in Java?
items.a: Java caches Integer objects for values -128 to 127. valueOf() and autoboxing return the same cached object in this range, so == returns true. For values outside this range, new objects are created and == returns false. Always use .equals() to compare Integer values — never ==. Same caching applies to Byte, Short, Long (-128 to 127) and Character (0 to 127). Boolean always caches TRUE and FALSE. Double and Float have no cache.

items.q: What is the difference between int and Integer in Java?
items.a: int is a primitive: stored on stack, cannot be null, default 0, no methods, 4 bytes, fastest. Integer is an object: stored on heap, can be null, default null for fields, has utility methods, ~16 bytes. Use int for local variables and computations; use Integer for Collections, nullable values, and utility method access. int comparison with == is value-based (correct); Integer comparison with == is reference-based (use .equals() instead).

items.q: How do you convert String to int in Java?
items.a: Use Integer.parseInt(String) to get a primitive int: int n = Integer.parseInt('42'); — throws NumberFormatException for invalid strings. Use Integer.valueOf(String) to get an Integer object. For int → String: use String.valueOf(42) or Integer.toString(42). Always wrap parseInt in try-catch when the input may not be a valid number.
